What's In The Drawer: An Update on the PMM AI Tool Stack

The survey numbers, the three tiers of access, the headliner tools, and the twelve-week plan to get there. A field guide for the D&A team — and anyone running a similar play.

By Chris O'Hara SAP D&A Offsite · Dallas · April 2026

Eight of the twenty-eight PMMs on our team who answered the offsite survey are paying out of pocket — fifty to a hundred dollars a month, in some cases more — for AI tools that, in several cases, SAP already provides for free or close to it. That number is not in the deck to make anyone feel bad; it's there because it tells you almost everything you need to know about the current state of AI adoption inside large enterprises, which is that the tools have moved faster than the internal communication about the tools, which in turn has moved faster than the training, which has moved faster than anyone's actual workflow, and the result is a team that is spending real money to solve problems someone else on a different floor solved last quarter.

The two top blockers on the survey came in almost identical in shape — "I don't know what's available" was first, and "I can't get access" was second, and the difference between them is mostly a question of which floor you happen to sit on. So this article is the drawer, opened and labeled.

Before we get into the inventory, the reason the inventory matters has shifted under our feet, and it's worth a paragraph. Search became an answer — Google gave ten blue links, LLMs give one, and that one increasingly belongs to a competitor. Buyers arrive having read three AI summaries of our category before we ever get on the call, which means the generic content we shipped last year is being paraphrased into irrelevance by the very models our prospects are using to read about us. And the deliverables themselves have changed shape — briefs, decks, battlecards are now mostly co-drafted with agents, which means the durable PMM work has moved up the stack, from typing and formatting to thinking and shaping. None of which is news to anyone who's been awake; all of which is the reason the right tools, in the right hands, with the right amount of practice, matter more this year than they did last.

The current inventory sorts into three tiers, and the first thing to know is that the tiers have nothing to do with quality. They're about access friction.

Tier 1 Enterprise-Approved
Low risk · Scalable · Preferred. Provisioned centrally by SAP. If you have an SAP login, you have access. The default and the path of least resistance.
Copilot Chat · GenAI Experience Lab · CompeteGPT · ReferenceGPT · Claude Code · Joule · EKX
Tier 2 Budget-Approved
Moderate control · Department-managed. Requires a budget request and SAM approval. The process is real but not painful, and the people who use them well usually decided thirty days ago that they were going to.
Perplexity Pro · Comet Browser · Adobe AI · Canva · Synthesia · Copilot in-app (Word / PowerPoint / Teams)
Tier 3 Pilot & Non-Onboarded
Higher risk · Limited visibility · Six-to-nine month onboarding. Watch but don't onboard yourself. Strong opinions go to the AI Champs network, not into a personal account.
Crayon · Writer · Clozd · Copy.ai · Beautiful.ai

The standing rule across all three tiers is the one that keeps lawyers calm: no personal or customer data into anything that hasn't been cleared, no proprietary code in unapproved tools, and always review AI output before sharing. Treat that as the floor, not a suggestion.

The drawer is fuller than the team thinks it is. Most of the gap isn't budget. It's awareness.

A few of the Tier 1 tools are worth a closer look, because the difference between "knowing the tool exists" and "knowing what it's actually for" is exactly the gap this article is trying to close.

Joule is your front door for SAP-specific transactions and answers — when you need a product feature explained, a customer-facing process guided, or a transactional task completed inside an SAP product, Joule is the path the company has invested in and the path our customers will see. Joule for Consultants is the field-and-customer-facing variant. If you've never logged in, the right move this week is to log in and ask it five questions about your own product area; the muscle memory is the whole game.

Copilot Chat is the workhorse — free, integrated across the M365 suite (Edge browser, M365.com, the M365 Copilot app, the right-click "Summarize with Copilot" in Explorer), and the right default for any general-purpose task that doesn't require deep SAP-specific knowledge. Drafting an email, summarizing a Teams meeting, riffing on a tagline, brainstorming a brief structure, asking "explain this concept like I'm a first-year MBA" — all of it. The full Copilot license unlocks the in-app capabilities (Copilot in Word, in PowerPoint, in Teams), which is where Tier 2 enters the picture, but the free Chat version is more capable than people give it credit for.

The Generative AI Experience Lab is the playground — when you want to compare answers across foundation models, prototype a prompt, or try the PowerPoint generator on a deck topic, the Lab is where you go. Data protection is built in, multiple LLMs are available, and there's an iOS app, which has the practical effect of making the commute between meetings useful again.

Perplexity Pro (Tier 2) is the research tool — when you need real-time web answers with citations, when you need to scan ten competitor blog posts in five minutes, when you're triangulating a market claim and want sources attached, Perplexity is faster than the alternatives. Comet Browser, the AI-first browser that comes with it, is worth installing if you do this kind of work daily.

Claude Code is the wildcard, and the one most worth your attention even if you've never opened a terminal. Yes, it's an agentic coding assistant from Anthropic — it reads codebases, edits files, runs commands, opens pull requests. But it also writes interactive web artifacts, builds quick React prototypes, generates HTML for a battlecard or a microsite, manipulates spreadsheets at the command line, and does the kind of "I need a working thing by Friday" work that previously required borrowing a spare engineer for a half-day. Two function leads — Kara on technical PMM, Brian on commercialization — are the test cases for getting this into broader PMM hands. Watch their unit closely.

EKX, which I wrote about in a separate piece, sits adjacent to all of this — it's the SAP knowledge graph in chat form, behind ekx.cloud.sap/chat, and it's the right tool when the question is "what is the actual current SAP truth about X." Use it for the questions where ChatGPT will fluently make things up.

· · ·

Knowing the drawer exists is half the work. Using it well is the other half, and that's what the curriculum is for.

The twelve-week plan is twelve weeks long, and not two days, because AI tools don't get internalized in workshops; they get internalized through repeat use against real work, ideally with someone watching over your shoulder for the first few attempts. The shape is: a team-wide foundation, then function-specific tracks, then a portfolio at the end where every PMM has produced enough new work in the new way that the new way is just the way.

Curriculum Map
From units to tools to teams
When Unit Tools Lands hardest for
Wk 1–2 Prompting + tool stack + governance Joule · Copilot Chat · GenAI Lab · CompeteGPT Everyone — baseline fluency
Wk 3 Drafting with pushback Copilot Chat · GenAI Lab Kaiser — Outbound
Wk 4 Research + competitive synthesis Perplexity Pro + CompeteGPT Olivier — Research · Tony — BDC
Wk 5 Function-specific co-working Tool mix varies by track Brian · Kara · Kaiser · Tony
Wk 6–8 Interactive artifacts (React) Claude Code Kara — Technical · Brian — Commercialization
Wk 9–10 Agent workflows Claude Code + Copilot Chat Tony — BDC · Katryn & Stuart — Field/Partner
Wk 11–12 Portfolio + graduation Full stack Every PMM

The note for function leads: every unit has a team it lands hardest for, and that's the one to show up to, coach through, and demo from. Don't try to be present at all twelve weeks for everyone. Be present at the one week where your team needs you most, and let the rest of the curriculum carry the rest.

The note for everyone else: the curriculum is a path, not a gate. Nothing in this article requires you to wait twelve weeks. The Tier 1 tools are open right now. The Tier 2 process is real but tractable. The survey told us 68% of the team wants training, which means 32% are ready to go without it — if you're in that 32%, go.

→ The action item, if there's only one If you're spending personal money on a tool that's already in Tier 1, stop. If you can't tell whether it is, ask. The drawer is fuller than the team thinks it is, the curriculum is on its way, and the gap between "knows what's available" and "uses what's available" is the only one that matters now.
